newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deputies back new arms cuts, oppose START.
newsitem.headline: Russian deputies back new arms cuts, oppose START.

text.p: Russian legislators on Thursday welcomed a report that the United States wanted new cuts in strategic nuclear arms despite remaining largely opposed to the unratified START-2 treaty.

Quoting unidentified senior U.S. officials, the Washington Post on Thursday reported Washington would seek cuts well beyond the roughly 50 percent reduction set by U.S. and Russian leaders in 1993 as the 10-year goal to be reached under START-2.
The head of the security committee in the Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, said he favoured more disarmament talks with the United States.
"Of course, we must reduce the level of armaments. But the United States should allow Russia to decide by itself the (weapon) systems it will reduce," Viktor Ilyukhin said.
"We can't allow a one-sided disarmament of Russia, especially on the condition that NATO expands to the east."
Russia is fiercely opposed to the western alliance's plans to take in new members in central and eastern Europe.
START-2, which was concluded in January 1993, is unpopular among Russian lawmakers who say it is unfair to Moscow and forces them to cut their most modern weapons systems.
The agreement is not on the current Duma session's agenda, and observers say at present it has little chance of passing.

Vladimir Lukin, a political moderate who heads the Duma's international affairs committee, said: "START-3 is not a bad idea if we can go ahead without the ratification of START-2. But I don't really believe that is possible."
The Post report said the U.S. proposal for new cuts was seen by some American officials as a way to persuade Russian legislators to ratify START-2, the Post said.

A secret U.S. Defence Department study is now examining the military consequences of ordering as many as 1,000 to 1,500 additional nuclear warheads to be scrapped on both sides, according to the report.
That could leave residual forces of as few as 2,000 weapons, about the level of the U.S. nuclear arsenal in 1956.
Alexei Podberoskin, a communist deputy who heads the subcommittee on intelligence matters, said START-3 talks should be part of wider talks on NATO and conventional disarmament.
"In principle, it's a good idea to throw away START-2 and go right to START-3, but START-3 should be connected with America fulfilling different conditions," he told Reuters.

"To begin with, we need to see exactly what the Americans are proposing in START-3 negotiations, because only (ex-Soviet President Mikhail) Gorbachev could go abroad without specifics, not knowing what agreement he would sign," he said.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin is scheduled to travel to the United States in March to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton.
